# SiC MOSFET double-pulse test in simulation (onsemi NTH4L022N120M3S)

I simulated the standard double-pulse switching test of a 1200 V, 22 mΩ SiC MOSFET with
the manufacturer's SPICE model, checked the switching energies against the datasheet,
and used the checked set-up to size the gate resistors, the power-loop inductance budget
and the Kelvin-source benefit.

> Simulation only: LTspice with onsemi's encrypted vendor model. Nothing here was measured
> on hardware. Independent project, not affiliated with or endorsed by onsemi.

| Turn-off peak dv/dt ≤ 50 V/ns | needs Rg,off ≥ 15 Ω: Eon + Eoff + Err ×1.9, mostly from induced conduction of the free-wheeling device |
| LTspice convergence aid `cshunt` | 1e-15 F inflates Eon ×6.0; the values used change it by ≤ 1.0 % |

## Method

![Double-pulse test circuit](docs/figures/dpt_circuit.svg)

| Item | Choice |
|---|---|
| DUT | NTH4L022N120M3S, 1200 V, 22 mΩ, TO-247-4L (Kelvin source pin) |
| Model | onsemi physical scalable LTspice model, 4-pin isothermal variant, library v2.3 |
| Free-wheeling device | same part, body diode, gate held at -3 V through Rg,off (the datasheet condition) |
| Gate drive | ideal -3 V / +18 V source, 5 ns edges, separate Rg,on and Rg,off |
| Parasitics | external power loop Lloop (split above and below the half-bridge); package inductances inside the model; optional extra common-source inductance Lcs |
| Load | 100 µH, first pulse sized so the current at turn-off is the target |
| Simulator | LTspice 26.0.1, batch mode, Alternate solver |
| Nominal point | 800 V, 40 A, Rg = 4.5 Ω, Lloop = 30 nH, 25 °C, Kelvin drive |

1. **Model checks.** RDS(on) at 25 °C and 175 °C and a resistive-load turn-on, before any
   switching run. The 1200 V model passes; the 650 V sister part's model shows a
   non-physical 600 ns turn-on delay in this LTspice version and is excluded.
2. **Convergence aid.** The model only converges with LTspice's `cshunt` option, and the
   common 1 fF setting corrupts the turn-on. I swept it and use a value on the plateau
   ([DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md#6-convergence-the-cshunt-trap)).
3. **Validation.** The datasheet Eon / Eoff condition, over a 10 nH to 50 nH loop
   bracket because the datasheet does not state its test-board inductance, plus an
   error budget for the deviation.
4. **Sweeps.** Rg,on, Rg,off, loop inductance, bus voltage, current, temperature, off-state
   gate voltage, Kelvin vs non-Kelvin drive.
5. **Extraction** (`dpt.extract`, unit-tested on synthetic waveforms with known answers).
   Energies are integrated from terminal waveforms, as a hardware DPT would see them:
   Eon from 10 % of the gate swing to vDS = 2 % of Vbus, Eoff from 90 % of the gate
   swing to iD = 2 % of the load current (IEC 60747-8 style; the datasheet does not
   publish its windows). Err is the free-wheeling device's energy from current reversal
   to the end of recovery.

## Validation against the datasheet

<!-- BEGIN validation (generated by python -m dpt.run_all; do not edit) -->

Datasheet condition: 800 V, 40 A, Rg = 4.5 Ω, -3 V / +18 V, 25 °C, body diode of the same part as free-wheeler (NTH4L022N120M3S/D Rev. 9).

| Loop L | Eon sim / ds (µJ) | Eon dev. | Eoff sim / ds (µJ) | Eoff dev. | Eon + Eoff sim / ds (µJ) | Eon + Eoff dev. |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10 nH | 566 / 490 | +16 % | 147 / 221 | -34 % | 713 / 711 | 0 % |
| 20 nH | 511 / 490 | +4 % | 157 / 221 | -29 % | 667 / 711 | -6 % |
| 30 nH | 449 / 490 | -8 % | 166 / 221 | -25 % | 614 / 711 | -14 % |
| 50 nH | 326 / 490 | -33 % | 179 / 221 | -19 % | 505 / 711 | -29 % |

**Error budget at the nominal point** (change of each quantity relative to the nominal simulation):

| Input changed from the nominal set-up | How | Eon | Eoff | Eon + Eoff |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Driver output resistance +1 Ω on both edges | simulated | +11 % | +17 % | +13 % |
| Gate-loop inductance 10 nH | simulated | -9 % | -4 % | -8 % |
| External loop inductance 10 nH | simulated (validation bracket) | +26 % | -12 % | +16 % |
| External loop inductance 20 nH | simulated (validation bracket) | +14 % | -6 % | +9 % |
| External loop inductance 50 nH | simulated (validation bracket) | -27 % | +8 % | -18 % |
| Current probe 1 ns late (deskew error) | re-extracted | -11 % | +15 % | -4 % |
| Current probe 1 ns early (deskew error) | re-extracted | +11 % | -14 % | +4 % |
| Eon window ends at 10 % of Vbus instead of 2 % | re-extracted | -1 % | 0 % | 0 % |
| Eoff window ends at 10 % of iD instead of 2 % | re-extracted | 0 % | -1 % | 0 % |
| cshunt 1e-19 F instead of 1e-21 F | simulated (convergence study) | +1 % | -1 % | 0 % |
| cshunt 1e-22 F instead of 1e-21 F | simulated (convergence study) | 0 % | 0 % | 0 % |

How to read it. No single input above closes the -25 % Eoff gap on its own. Two things the ideal set-up lacks each move Eoff by a large part of it: 1 Ω of driver output resistance raises Eoff by +17 % (the swept Rg,off reproduces the datasheet Eoff at about 6.4 Ω instead of 4.5 Ω), and a current probe 1 ns late raises the measured Eoff by +15 %. Together they would account for the gap, but neither can be confirmed without the datasheet bench. The deskew error also lowers Eon (-11 %) and leaves Eon + Eoff almost unchanged (-4 %): timing errors shift energy between the two edges. onsemi's own DPT board manual shows the same on hardware: changing only the current sensor moved Eon from 431 to 224 µJ and Eoff from 141 to 296 µJ, while Eon + Eoff changed by -9 % (EVBUM2897/D, Table 4; 600 V, Rg = 3.9 Ω). Eon + Eoff is therefore the more trustworthy comparison, and the loop inductance, which the datasheet does not state, is the largest single unknown.

<!-- END validation -->

![Simulated Eon, Eoff and Eon + Eoff vs loop inductance, with the datasheet values](docs/figures/validation.png)

## Design takeaways

<!-- BEGIN takeaways (generated by python -m dpt.run_all; do not edit) -->

- **Rg,on.** Eon + Err stays between 704 and 722 µJ from 1 Ω to 4.5 Ω: a faster turn-on lowers Eon but raises the free-wheeling device's recovery energy by almost as much. Keeping its recovery overshoot ≤ 960 V needs Rg,on ≥ 10 Ω. No swept Rg,on meets 50 V/ns peak dv/dt (lowest 70 V/ns at 22 Ω): the last part of the vDS fall is the fast collapse at the end of the body-diode recovery (visible in the turn-on waveform), so the lever is the free-wheeling device or a snubber, not more gate resistance.
- **Rg,off.** Meeting 50 V/ns at turn-off with every peak ≤ 960 V needs Rg,off ≥ 15 Ω. Eoff alone rises from 166 to 494 µJ, but Eon + Eoff + Err rises from 882 to 1659 µJ: the free-wheeling device is held off through the same resistor, and its gate is pulled up to 7.9 V (VGS(th),min = 2.04 V) during the DUT turn-on, so it conducts briefly (its terminal Qrr rises from 568 to 1093 nC). A resistor-only design that limits dv/dt this way pays mainly in shoot-through; a separate low-impedance hold-off path (Miller clamp) is needed.
- **Off-state bias.** At -3 V the free-wheeling device's gate reaches 4.47 V during DUT turn-on, above VGS(th),min = 2.04 V. -5 V restores a +0.76 V margin (Err 268 → 219 µJ), but the gate then undershoots to -10.56 V at DUT turn-off, beyond the -10 V rating. Bias alone does not fix it; an active Miller clamp is the next thing to simulate.
- **Stray inductance.** Every vDS peak stays ≤ 960 V up to 16.1 nH of external loop inductance. The free-wheeling device's recovery overshoot sets that limit; the DUT turn-off peak alone would allow 25.0 nH, so a layout review that only checks the DUT turn-off spike accepts a loop that overstresses the other device.
- **Kelvin source.** Returning the driver to the power source pin puts the package source inductance into the gate loop: at equal Rg, Eon + Eoff rises by 48 % and Eon + Eoff + Err by 18 % (the slower turn-on lowers Err). Equal Rg is not equal speed, though: against a Kelvin-driven DUT slowed to the same turn-on di/dt (4.31 A/ns, Rg,on ≈ 8.0 Ω), the Eon penalty is 19 % instead of 56 %. With 10 nH of extra shared inductance the gate loop oscillates beyond the gate rating.

<!-- END takeaways -->

![Gate-resistor trade-off](docs/figures/rg_tradeoff.png)

## Limitations

- **No hardware.** The validation compares with datasheet *typical* values from a bench
  whose loop inductance, probes and deskew are not published.
- **Ideal gate driver.** No output resistance or propagation delay, and no gate-loop
  inductance except in the error budget. This is the main reason Eoff comes out low.
- **Encrypted vendor model.** Its internals cannot be inspected. Accuracy above
  V(BR)DSS (the large-loop recovery peaks exceed 1200 V) and avalanche are not assessed.
- **Isothermal.** The 4-pin model has no self-heating; temperature is a parameter. The
  6-pin thermal variant does not run with the Alternate solver (singular matrix).
- **Terminal quantities.** As on a real bench, the DUT's own Coss energy at turn-on is not
  visible at the terminals, and Err / Qrr include the free-wheeler's Coss charge, so they
  are not comparable with the datasheet Qrr and Erec (measured at 1 A/ns).
- **One simulator.** The model exists only encrypted for LTspice and PSpice, so ngspice
  could not cross-check it. Results depend on `cshunt` until it is small enough; the
  convergence study shows where that is.
- **One typical device.** No model corners or part-to-part spread.

## Next steps

- Simulate an active Miller clamp on the free-wheeling device: it is the fix that both the
  Rg,off and the off-state-bias results point to.
- Add a driver model (output resistance, delay, gate-loop inductance) and redo the
  validation.
- Repeat the Rg,off and stray-inductance budgets at 175 °C.
- Report the 650 V model's turn-on delay to onsemi's model support.

## Reproduce

Tested on Windows 11 with LTspice 26.0.1 and Python 3.12.10. LTspice for macOS has the
same batch mode, but this pipeline has not been run there.

1. Install [LTspice](https://www.analog.com/ltspice). If it is not in the default
   location, set `LTSPICE_EXE` to the executable.
2. Create the environment and install the pinned dependencies.

   ```powershell
   # Windows PowerShell (if scripts are blocked, first run
   # Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope Process RemoteSigned)
   py -3.12 -m venv .venv
   .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
   ```

   ```bash
   # Git Bash on Windows; on macOS use python3.12 and .venv/bin/activate
   py -3.12 -m venv .venv
   source .venv/Scripts/activate
   ```

   Then, in either shell:

   ```bash
   python -m pip install -r requirements-lock.txt
   python -m pip install -e . --no-deps
   ```

3. Fetch the onsemi models (not redistributable, see [Licence](#licence)). The script
   downloads them from onsemi, checks their SHA256 and unpacks them; if the download is
   refused it prints the product page and file name to save by hand into
   `third_party/onsemi/`.

   ```bash
   python -m dpt.fetch_models
   ```

4. Run the checks and the study.

   ```bash
   python -m pytest -q        # unit tests, no simulator needed
   python -m dpt.run_all      # 8 to 12 min from an empty cache on a laptop
   ```

`run_all` rewrites `results/`, `docs/figures/`, `docs/results.md` and the generated blocks
of this README; on a fresh clone with the same model version the diff is empty. Each
simulation is cached in `build/sim/<config hash>/` with its netlist, log and raw file, so
any run can be opened in LTspice by hand. `make all` runs the same steps where `make` is
available. Console output of these commands is in [docs/screenshots](docs/screenshots).

## Repository layout

```
src/dpt/
  netlist.py        DPT netlist generator (LTspice dialect), all circuit parameters
  ltspice.py        batch runner, cache, cshunt retry ladder
  rawread.py        binary .raw reader (LTspice and ngspice dialects)
  extract.py        Eon, Eoff, Err, dv/dt, di/dt, overshoot, ringing, gate bounce, times
  model_checks.py   RDS(on) and turn-on-delay checks per model
  devices.py        parts, pin orders, datasheet reference values (with sources)
  study.py          every simulated configuration, design limits, error-budget inputs
  analysis.py       budget and selection helpers
  run_all.py        one-command pipeline: simulations, CSVs, figures
  report.py         Markdown generated from results/summary.json
  fetch_models.py   download, verify and unpack the onsemi model ZIPs
tests/              pytest: extraction, raw reader, netlist, analysis
results/            one CSV per sweep, error_budget.csv, summary.json
docs/               results.md, figures, console screenshots
DESIGN.md           decisions, dead ends and definitions
```
